scripts.radio:
Hamjambo wasikilizaji, karibuni kwa Kenya on Record. This week, we are looking at something sitting right inside your pocket: your mobile phone.

Currently, bringing a basic smartphone into Kenya attracts hefty levies, chief among them the 25% import and excise burden on fully built units. There is now a growing push to scrap this tax entirely to make smart devices truly affordable for ordinary citizens.

Here is the accountability question: how do we reconcile government’s ambition for a digital highway with policies that make the vehicle too expensive to buy? The state wants every mwananchi to access e-Citizen, file documents, and run businesses online. Yet, when an entry-level smartphone that should cost eight thousand shillings retails at twelve thousand because of border taxes, millions are locked out of the digital economy.

Treasury may argue that this levy protects local assembly plants and generates revenue. But taxing connectivity is short-sighted. An unconnected citizen cannot participate in modern trade or access digitized public services. The real long-term economic dividend lies in what people do once they are connected, not in punishing them at the port of entry.

Kwa ufupi: Kupunguza au kuondoa ushuru wa asilimia 25 kwa simu za rununu kutafanya bei ishuke ili kila mwananchi apate uwezo wa kujiunga na huduma za serikali na kufanya biashara mtandaoni bila vikwazo.

This is Kenya on Record. Let us keep the leaders accountable.
scripts.voice_note: Habari zenu. Quick thought from Kenya on Record this week. We talk about digitising government services—from e-Citizen to farm subsidies—yet buying an ordinary smartphone still carries a heavy 25% tax penalty. That means before a mama mboga or a young hustler even downloads an app or accesses an online portal, they are paying a steep entry fee just to own the screen. If digital access is an essential public infrastructure, why is the tool to access it taxed like a luxury? Revenue collection is important, but leaving millions offline because handsets are unaffordable slows down the entire economy. Scrapping this tax isn't a favour; it's common sense. Share this note, and let us demand policies that actually support digital inclusion.
scripts.sms: USIIBIWE: High phone taxes push fake gadgets into the market. Before buying a device, dial *#06# to get the IMEI, then verify it via SMS to 1555 for free.
scripts.reels: You cannot digitise a country while overtaxing the very tools needed to get online. A 25% tax on imported smartphones is simply a barrier between wananchi and essential services. From finding work to paying for healthcare and accessing e-Citizen, a smartphone is basic infrastructure, not a luxury. Cut the tax, lower device prices, and let ordinary Kenyans participate in the digital economy. Let's keep the record straight.
